artStyle: Glossy 1990s Japanese plastic model-kit toy style: smooth injection-moulded plastic, bold saturated colours, crisp panel lines and chunky round bolts, clean simple shapes, soft studio lighting.
notes: No person entries: every robot is built from parts moved in code (no bones, no Tripo animations).
Robot part names map to the game's slots: head -> head, core -> core, right_arm -> arm_r, left_arm -> arm_l, hips + legs/treads/skirt -> legs.
'right' and 'left' always mean the robot's own right and left. In a front view the robot's right arm is on the viewer's left.
hit_spark and part_debris are effects made in code and have no entry.

The four robots were made in Tripo Studio with these settings: image first, then HD Model -> H3.1 -> Generate in Parts (Simple), Ultra mesh quality, 30000 triangles; AI Completion to fill the parts; 4K texture plus PBR; the Mecha Pop and Wood styles are 4K plus PBR too. Export GLB with Pack UV off. The finished robots have about 41-43k triangles each.

entries.prompt: Glossy 1990s Japanese plastic model-kit toy style: smooth injection-moulded plastic, bold saturated colours, crisp panel lines and chunky round bolts, clean simple shapes, soft studio lighting. A small friendly toy battle robot standing straight and facing the viewer, about one and a half times as tall as it is wide. A boxy blue head, about a quarter of the total height, with two round yellow eyes on the front and one thin antenna ending in a small bell. A white box-shaped chest, as wide as the shoulders, with a round yellow chest light. The arms hang straight down at the sides, attached at round shoulder joints and slightly apart from the body, and end at mid-thigh: the robot's own right arm (on the viewer's left) is red and ends in a chunky square fist on a short coil spring; the robot's own left arm (on the viewer's right) is yellow and shaped like a short cork-gun barrel pointing down. A dark grey hip block, then two separate straight blue legs with flat white feet, standing slightly apart; the legs are about two fifths of the total height. The head, chest, each arm, the hips and each leg are separate pieces, each in its own single main colour; each piece fits snugly against the next with a crisp panel seam, no empty gaps. Fine toy details: engraved panel lines, small recessed screws at the corners, vents on the chest sides, and simple sticker-like stripe and chevron decals with no text. single isolated object, centered, on a plain white background

busiestMoment.when: A fight: both robots on screen, the toy box, 10 toy blocks, up to 6 corks and 2 rockets in the air; broken parts flying off are pieces of the robots already counted.

triangles.robots: 2 x 10,000 = 20,000 (a mixed robot built from 4 different models is still about one robot's worth)

textureMemory.assumption: Tripo exports up to 3 maps per model (colour, metal/roughness, normal). One map at 1024 px with mipmaps = 5.6 MB; at 512 px = 1.4 MB. Each robot's styles are separate texture sets.
textureMemory.worstCase: Pipo can wear parts from up to 5 different model/paint combinations plus the rival's 1 = 6 robot texture sets on screen.
textureMemory.loadPlan: Robots and the toy box are downscaled to 1024 px when loaded (a robot is at most about 300 px tall on screen, so 2K adds nothing visible); the block, cork and rocket to 512 px. On phones, normal maps are skipped (smooth plastic barely needs them).
textureMemory.drawCalls: about 7 pieces per robot (one material each) x 2 + arena + 10 blocks + projectiles = about 40, about 80 with shadows

busiestMoment.phoneVerdict: Yes. About 31,000 triangles and about 87 MB of textures is well within what a phone from the last 5 years handles at 60 fps. It depends on shrinking the 2K textures when loading, which the swap stage will do.
